pattern.none: built with the ending ־ִית on the root ת־כ־ן (as in תִּכְנֵן “to plan”), not one of the common patterns

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

lexemes.note: A plan (also a programme). Feminine; full spelling תוכנית.

profile.feeling: A list on the fridge, a map spread on the table before a trip.

examples.tr: What are your (m.) plans for the holidays?
I have a plan: we’ll go to Eilat.
The plan changed.

synonyms.nuance: “planning” — the activity, not the plan
“an intention” — what one means to do, less worked out

etymology.text: From the root ת־כ־ן, as in תִּכְנֵן “to plan” (which Wiktionary lists under “plan”), with the ending ־ִית; Wiktionary gives no etymology for the noun.

funFacts: The same word is a TV programme (תׇּכְנִית טֶלֶוִיזְיָה) and a computer program (Wiktionary’s senses); software is the related תׇּכְנָה.
pitfalls: The first vowel is a short o (qamats katan): tochnít; the everyday spelling is תוכנית (also written תכנית).
Wiktionary’s other senses — a TV or radio programme, a computer program, a business plan — use the same word: context decides.
subtleties: Plans for a weekend are usually plural: יֵשׁ לָנוּ תׇּכְנִיּוֹת לְסוֹף הַשָּׁבוּעַ.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

lexemes.note: A trip, an outing, a hike. Verbal noun of טִיֵּל.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses טִיּוּל as “tour, voyage; walk, hike”, none of which uses the words of the course gloss “trip, journey”; these are the same meaning (יָצָאנוּ לְטִיּוּל “we went on a trip”).

profile.feeling: Backpacks, water bottles, a path in the hills of the Galilee.

senses.def: a trip, a tour, an outing; a hike, a walk

examples.tr: We went on a trip to the north.
How was the trip?

examples.text: אַחֲרֵי הַצָּבָא הוּא יָצָא לְטִיּוּל אָרֹךְ.
examples.tr: After the army he went on a long trip.

synonyms.nuance: “a ride, a journey” — the travelling itself, by vehicle
“a long journey, an expedition” (Wiktionary lists it as a synonym)
“a tour” — a guided visit of a site or a town

etymology.text: The verbal noun of טִיֵּל “to stroll, travel”, root ט־י־ל, in the pattern קִטּוּל (Wiktionary).

funFacts: After military service many young Israelis go on “the big trip”, הַטִּיּוּל הַגָּדוֹל, abroad for months.
pitfalls: A trip for pleasure; a business trip is a נְסִיעַת עֲסָקִים.
The י is a consonant and doubled: tiyúl (full spelling טיול).
subtleties: טִיּוּל is any outing — from a walk round the block to a month in India.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

construct.note: in names: מְלוֹן הַמֶּלֶךְ דָּוִד “the King David Hotel”

lexemes.note: A hotel. Masculine, plural מְלוֹנוֹת; also בֵּית מָלוֹן.

profile.feeling: A reception desk, a key card, breakfast on the terrace.

examples.tr: We booked a room in a hotel by the sea.
The hotel was clean and nice.
Which hotel are you (pl.) staying at?

synonyms.nuance: the fuller form, the same meaning (Wiktionary lists both as synonyms)
“a hostel, an inn” (אַכְסַנְיַת נֹעַר “youth hostel”)
a guest cabin in the countryside, from German Zimmer

etymology.text: From the root ל־ו־ן of לָן “to lodge, stay the night” (Wiktionary: “see לָן”).

funFacts: The root is “to spend the night”: a מָלוֹן is a place to lodge, like the biblical מָלוֹן “lodging place”.
pitfalls: Three words share the everyday spelling מלון: מָלוֹן “hotel”, מֶלוֹן “melon” — and the full spelling of מִלּוֹן “dictionary” is מילון (Wiktionary).
Masculine with a plural in -וֹת: מְלוֹנוֹת גְּדוֹלִים.
subtleties: Staying at a hotel is גָּר בְּמָלוֹן or, more precisely, לָן בְּמָלוֹן “spends the night at a hotel”.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: To book, reserve; to order; to invite. Hif‘il of ז־מ־ן: past הִזְמִין / הִזְמַנְתִּי, present מַזְמִין, future יַזְמִין, infinitive לְהַזְמִין. Noun: הַזְמָנָה.

override.meaning: Wiktionary’s glosses of הִזְמִין (“to invite; to order: to request a product or service”) do not contain the words of the course gloss “to book, to reserve”; booking a room or a table is requesting a service, the standard use (הִזְמַנּוּ חֶדֶר בְּמָלוֹן).

profile.feeling: A phone call to a hotel, a waiter with a notepad, a wedding invitation in the post.

senses.def: to book, reserve (a room, a table, tickets)

examples.tr: I booked a room for three nights.
Have you (pl.) already booked tickets?
I ordered a pizza (to the house).
Can we order?
They invited us to the wedding.
I’m inviting you (pl.) to dinner.

synonyms.nuance: “to keep a place” — informally, for someone
“to make an appointment” — a doctor, a hairdresser

etymology.text: Hif‘il of the root ז־מ־ן, the root of זְמַן “time” (Wiktionary gives no etymology; its senses are “to invite” and “to order: to request a product or service”). The verbal noun הַזְמָנָה is a booking, an order and an invitation.

funFacts: One noun for three things: הַזְמָנָה is a hotel booking, an order in a shop and a wedding invitation.
pitfalls: The present starts with מַ־ (hif‘il): מַזְמִין, מַזְמִינָה.
In the past the i becomes a before the endings of the 1st and 2nd person: הִזְמִין but הִזְמַנְתִּי, and in “we” the two נ merge: הִזְמַנּוּ.
Inviting someone takes the person as object and the event with לְ: הִזְמִינוּ אוֹתָנוּ לַחֲתֻנָּה.
subtleties: Which meaning? A room or a table → booked; food or a taxi → ordered; a person → invited.

pattern.none: the noun דֶּרֶךְ “way” + the ending ־וֹן, not a pattern (Wiktionary)

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

profile.feeling: The airport queue, a stamp, the panic of “where is it?”.

examples.tr: Don’t forget the passport!
My passport is no longer valid.
She has two passports.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in everyday use; the identity card תְּעוּדַת זֶהוּת is another document.

etymology.text: דֶּרֶךְ “way, road” + the ending ־וֹן (Wiktionary): “the document for the road”.

funFacts: A modern coinage built from “way”: the passport is the “road document”.
pitfalls: Not the identity card: that is תְּעוּדַת זֶהוּת (ת״ז).
The construct plural is דַּרְכּוֹנֵי: דַּרְכּוֹנֵי הַיְּלָדִים “the children’s passports”.
subtleties: Valid = בְּתֹקֶף, expired = לֹא בְּתֹקֶף or פָּג תֹּקֶף.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

lexemes.note: A suitcase. Feminine; full spelling מזוודה.

profile.feeling: Packing the night before, wheels rattling through the terminal.

examples.tr: I packed the suitcase at night.
The suitcase is too heavy.
Where are our suitcases?

synonyms.nuance: “a bag” — smaller, carried in the hand or on the back

etymology.text: A noun of the pattern מִקְטָלָה (Wiktionary) on the root ז־ו־ד; Wiktionary gives no further etymology.

funFacts: The ו is a consonant: miz-va-da — which is why the everyday spelling doubles it, מזוודה.
pitfalls: The consonant ו is doubled in everyday spelling: מזוודה, מזוודות.
Feminine: מִזְוָדָה כְּבֵדָה.
subtleties: The construct changes the vowels: מִזְוֶדֶת עוֹר “a leather suitcase”.

root.none: a fixed phrase of three words (חוּץ + לְ + הָאָרֶץ)

pattern.none: a fixed phrase, not one pattern

plurals.none: a name for “the world outside Israel”: no plural

construct.none: a fixed phrase: not put into the construct

lexemes.note: Abroad — the world outside Israel. Used like a place name (no article): לְחוּץ לָאָרֶץ, בְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ; colloquially חוּ״ל.

profile.feeling: Departures board at Ben Gurion airport; relatives “in chul”.

senses.def: abroad, foreign countries (the world outside Israel)

examples.tr: She lives abroad.
We went abroad in the summer.
He came back from abroad.

synonyms.nuance: the abbreviation, said chul — the everyday word: נוֹסְעִים לְחוּ״ל (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: From חוּץ “outside” + לְ־ + הָאָרֶץ “the land”: literally “outside of the country”; a fixed expression from Mishnaic Hebrew (Wiktionary).

funFacts: הָאָרֶץ, “the land”, means Israel here; Israelis say בָּאָרֶץ “in the country” for Israel and בְּחוּ״ל for everywhere else.
pitfalls: It behaves like a place name: no article, and the preposition goes in front — לְחוּץ לָאָרֶץ “(to) abroad”, בְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ “(in) abroad”, מֵחוּץ לָאָרֶץ “from abroad”.
Masculine (Wiktionary), but it is rarely the subject of a sentence.
subtleties: The point of view is Israel’s: for a speaker in Israel, every other country is חוּ״ל.

lexemes.note: To visit. Pi‘el: past בִּקֵּר / בִּקַּרְתִּי (full spelling ביקר), present מְבַקֵּר, future יְבַקֵּר, infinitive לְבַקֵּר. A place with בְּ.

profile.feeling: Grandma’s door on Saturday, a museum on a holiday, flowers for someone in hospital.

senses.def: to visit (a place: בְּ; a person: אֶת, colloquially אֵצֶל)

examples.tr: In the summer we visited Rome.
We visited Grandma in hospital.
Come and visit!

synonyms.nuance: “to pop over, drop in” — a short visit (קָפַצְתִּי אֵלֶיהָ)
“to tour, go round” — a site, a town

etymology.text: Pi‘el of the root ב־ק־ר (Wiktionary gives no etymology; its senses are “to visit”, “to inspect” and “to criticize”). The noun is בִּקּוּר “visit”.

funFacts: A מְבַקֵּר is both a visitor and a critic — the verb also means “to criticize”.
pitfalls: A place takes בְּ: בִּקַּרְנוּ בְּרוֹמָא — not *בִּקַּרְנוּ רוֹמָא.

Wiktionary also gives “to inspect” and “to criticize” (בִּקֵּר אֶת הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה “criticized the government”): with a person as object, context decides between visiting and criticizing — in speech, visiting a person is usually בִּקֵּר אֵצֶל.
subtleties: The past has i in the first syllable (full spelling ביקר, ביקרתי); the present מְבַקֵּר has none.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

lexemes.note: A tourist (a man). A woman: תַּיֶּרֶת. Plural תַּיָּרִים.

contrasts.value: a man (the plural also for a mixed group)

profile.feeling: Cameras in the Old City, maps unfolded on a street corner.

senses.def: a tourist (a man; the plural also for a mixed group)

examples.tr: There are lots of tourists in Jerusalem.
The tourist asked me where the station is.

examples.text: אֲנַחְנוּ לֹא תַּיָּרִים, אֲנַחְנוּ גָּרִים פֹּה.
examples.tr: We aren’t tourists, we live here.

synonyms.nuance: “a traveller, hiker” — someone on a trip, also at home
“a visitor” — to a site, a museum, a country

etymology.text: From the root ת־י־ר / ת־ו־ר “to explore, scout” in the pattern קַטָּל, the pattern of trades (Wiktionary). The spies of Numbers 13 were sent “to scout” (לָתוּר) the land.

funFacts: Tourism is תַּיָּרוּת — the same root as the biblical spies who “scouted” the land.
pitfalls: A woman is a תַּיֶּרֶת; a mixed group is תַּיָּרִים.
The י is doubled: tayár (full spelling תייר).
subtleties: An Israeli travelling in Israel is a מְטַיֵּל, not a תַּיָּר.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

construct.none: not used in the construct in everyday Hebrew

override.meaning: Wiktionary has no entry for תיירת; the check falls back to the full spelling of the plural, תיירות, which is also the noun “tourism” (Wiktionary lists תיירת as the feminine counterpart of תַּיָּר).

profile.feeling: A woman with a backpack and a guidebook asking the way.

examples.tr: A tourist from Germany photographed the Western Wall.
The (women) tourists came by bus.
One tourist (f.) asked about the hotel.

synonyms.nuance: “a traveller, hiker (f.)” — someone on a trip, also at home

etymology.text: The feminine of תַּיָּר (Wiktionary lists תיירת as its feminine counterpart), with the ending ־ֶת.

funFacts: The ending ־ֶת makes the ־ָ־ of תַּיָּר an ־ֶ־: tayéret.
pitfalls: Women only: a group with one man is תַּיָּרִים.
subtleties: The plural goes back to the vowel of the masculine: תַּיָּרוֹת.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

lexemes.note: A guide (a man); also an instructor, a guidebook. A woman: מַדְרִיכָה.

contrasts.value: a man (the plural also for a mixed group)

profile.feeling: A raised umbrella at the head of a group, stories at every corner.

senses.def: a guide (a man; the plural also for a mixed group)

examples.text: הַמַּדְרִיךְ הִסְבִּיר לָנוּ עַל הָעִיר הָעַתִּיקָה.
examples.tr: The guide told us about the Old City.
He works as a tour guide.
There were two guides on the trip.

synonyms.nuance: “one who shows the way” — a (licensed) guide (Wiktionary lists it under “guide”)

etymology.text: The present participle of הִדְרִיךְ “to guide”, root ד־ר־ך “way”, in the pattern מַקְטִיל (Wiktionary): “the one who shows the way”.

funFacts: דֶּרֶךְ “way” gives the guide (מַדְרִיךְ), the passport (דַּרְכּוֹן) and the guidance (הַדְרָכָה).
pitfalls: Wiktionary’s other senses — a youth counsellor, an instructor, a guidebook — use the same word: context decides.
A woman is a מַדְרִיכָה.
subtleties: A tour guide is usually מַדְרִיךְ טִיּוּלִים; in the youth movements a מַדְרִיךְ is a group leader.

dual.none: no dual in use: “two” is שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural

profile.feeling: A guide with a microphone on the bus, counting heads.

examples.tr: The guide (f.) spoke English and Hebrew.
She is a tour guide.
The guides (f.) waited for the group.

synonyms.nuance: “one who shows the way” (f.) — a (licensed) guide

etymology.text: The feminine of מַדְרִיךְ (Wiktionary lists it as its feminine counterpart), root ד־ר־ך “way”.

funFacts: In the youth movements the מַדְרִיכָה is the leader of a group of children.
pitfalls: Women only: a group with one man is מַדְרִיכִים.
Construct: מַדְרִיכַת טִיּוּלִים (־ַת).

features.derivedFrom: בְּ + הַשָּׁבוּעַ “the week” + הַבָּא “the coming” (the present of בָּא with the article)

lexemes.note: Next week (adverb of time). As a subject: הַשָּׁבוּעַ הַבָּא. Last week: בַּשָּׁבוּעַ שֶׁעָבַר.

ref.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): no entry for the phrase; its words checked one by one

profile.feeling: The diary page after this one.

examples.tr: Next week we’ll go to Eilat.
See you next week!
The exam is next week.

synonyms.nuance: “in a week (from now)” — counted from today

antonyms.note: last week (“in the week that passed”)

etymology.text: A phrase: בְּ “in” + הַשָּׁבוּעַ “the week” + הַבָּא, the present (participle) of בָּא “to come” with the article — “in the coming week”. Wiktionary has no entry for the phrase.

funFacts: “Next” is “the coming one”: הַבָּא, הַבָּאָה — the verb בָּא used as an adjective.
pitfalls: As the subject there is no בְּ: הַשָּׁבוּעַ הַבָּא יִהְיֶה קָשֶׁה “next week will be hard”.
“Last week” is not built with אַחֲרוֹן: it is בַּשָּׁבוּעַ שֶׁעָבַר.
subtleties: הַבָּא agrees with its noun: הַשָּׁבוּעַ הַבָּא, הַשָּׁנָה הַבָּאָה, יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן הַבָּא “next Sunday”.

features.derivedFrom: בְּ + הַשָּׁנָה “the year” + הַבָּאָה “the coming” (feminine: שָׁנָה is feminine)

lexemes.note: Next year (adverb of time). Feminine agreement: הַבָּאָה. Last year: בַּשָּׁנָה שֶׁעָבְרָה.

ref.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): no entry for the phrase; its words checked one by one

profile.feeling: New Year’s resolutions; the Passover wish for Jerusalem.

examples.text: בַּשָּׁנָה הַבָּאָה אֲנִי אַתְחִיל לִלְמֹד בָּאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה.
examples.tr: Next year I’ll start studying at university.
Next year we’ll visit Greece.
The wedding will be next year.

phrases.meaning: the wish that closes the Passover Seder

synonyms.nuance: “in a year (from now)” — counted from today

etymology.text: A phrase: בְּ “in” + הַשָּׁנָה “the year” + הַבָּאָה, the feminine present (participle) of בָּא “to come” with the article. Wiktionary has no entry for the phrase.

funFacts: The Passover Seder ends with לְשָׁנָה הַבָּאָה בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם, “next year in Jerusalem”.
pitfalls: Feminine, because שָׁנָה is feminine: הַבָּאָה — and “last year” is בַּשָּׁנָה שֶׁעָבְרָה (feminine verb).
As the subject there is no בְּ: הַשָּׁנָה הַבָּאָה תִּהְיֶה טוֹבָה.
subtleties: With לְ it is a wish or a deadline: לְשָׁנָה הַבָּאָה “for next year”.
